newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: Waves of looters play cat and mouse with PNG police.
newsitem.headline: Waves of looters play cat and mouse with PNG police.

text.p: Waves of rock throwing looters attacked shops in Papua New Guinea's capital on Thursday in a cat-and-mouse game with riot police who repelled the attacks with tear gas, plastic bullets and live ammunition.
A machete-wielding security guard chopped off the hand of one young looter as the boy reached inside a broken shop door.
The looter ran away cradling his bloody stump wrapped in a brown T-shirt. His hand remained on the footpath for hours as police and rioters engaged in running battles.

Port Moresby, capital of the South Pacific nation of Papua New Guinea, was engulfed in civil unrest for a second day, with sporadic looting erupting around the city all day despite a heavy police presence.

What began on Monday as an army revolt against the government's use of African mercenaries to end the secessionist conflict on Bougainville island has turned into a social, political and military campaign against Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan.

"Life is bad here for many people and they do not like Sir Julius Chan," said Port Moresby resident Jack Kil, as 5,000 protesters waged a dangerous game with riot police armed with M16 automatic rifles outside the nation's army headquarters.
But while police struggled under the tropical sun to control rioters, the nation's army remained inside barracks.
As the crackle of live ammunition echoed across the sky, soldiers laid under the cool of trees reading newspaper reports of the looting and civil unrest.
Dressed in camouflage fatigues, wrap-around sunglasses, thongs (flip flops) and side arms, soldiers awaited the government's response to their demand that their sacked commander be reinstated.
Bridagier-General Jerry Singirok was sacked by Chan on Monday after he demanded the prime minister resign over the mercenary plan.

As police fired volleys over the heads of protesters outside Murray Barracks, thousands broke through the army's perimeter fence. Some dropped to the ground, disappearing in the thigh-high grass of the army's football field, popping their heads up minutes later once the shooting had stopped.
Other protesters, some women carrying children on their hips, ran towards the barracks but were herded back on to the street by soldiers eager not to give police an excuse to enter.

But tension between Papua New Guinea's army and police eventually spilled over into the barracks when police used the presence of protesters as an excuse to fire tear gas into a group of soldiers and fired shots over their heads.
A group of young soldiers tried to break into an armoury in an apparent attempt to return fire, but were stopped by senior officers.

As the confrontation between police and army erupted, high up on a hill inside Murray Barracks, with sweeping views of Port Moresby and the ocean, sat sacked army chief Singirok -- the man who sparked the unrest.

Dressed in a sports shirt and trousers, Singirok played with his pet dogs before holding a press conference in his backyard, again demanding Chan step down pending an inquiry into the hiring of mercenaries.
Singirok said he believed the deal with British-based Sandline International, a military consultancy, would have led to widespread civilian casualties on Bougainville.
While Chan has said the mercenaries would only act as advisers, Singirok insisted they would be in the frontline operating helicopter gunships on bombing raids.
Asked what would stop the civil unrest, Singirok said: "People will get hungry and go home -- this is Papua New Guinea".
